title: The Master Plan

jokes.text: Tom adds 'sexiest' to the newspaper description of the club, then immediately admits he added it himself
jokes.setup: Tom reads what sounds like an official newspaper quote calling the club 'the sexiest, most dangerous club in town'
jokes.punchline: He immediately confesses 'I added the word sexiest' — the grandiosity deflates instantly
jokes.explanation: Classic Tom Haverford self-aggrandizement punctured by immediate self-disclosure. The fast correction is perfectly timed and deeply character-specific — only Tom would brag about a quote, then admit he fabricated part of it without missing a beat.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm throwing this party because I'm a selfless friend who cares about my friends' happiness.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Just kidding. I'm using this party to meet women. Single women. Lots of them.

jokes.text: Tom declares he's a genius for using his friend's birthday party to 'stock the club with every available hottie I know' and predicts 'between one and four new girlfriends'
jokes.setup: Tom frames himself as a generous friend throwing a birthday party
jokes.punchline: The 'generosity' is entirely a pretext; his precise range of '1 to 4 new girlfriends' is absurdly specific and delusional
jokes.explanation: The specificity of '1 to 4' is the key comedic engine here — it sounds like a business projection, which makes Tom's romantic delusion funnier. Deeply Tom-specific humor; his self-serving altruism is a core character trait well-deployed.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I'm going to find my soulmate at this party. She's going to be between 5'2" and 5'11", probably work in marketing or nonprofit, definitely laugh at my jokes, and have zero emotional baggage.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Tom, that describes like three people in the entire city.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Exactly. Three chances. I like those odds.

jokes.text: Tom sarcastically says 'Oh, that's great. I'd love to hear all about your family vacations' when Kyle arrives at the party
jokes.setup: Tom is excited about the party full of 'hotties'; the door opens
jokes.punchline: Kyle — clearly a lame/unwanted presence — walks in, and Tom's enthusiasm immediately inverts into withering sarcasm
jokes.explanation: A solid quick joke. 'Family vacations' is a nice choice — the most boring possible topic — but the joke relies somewhat on the audience's pre-existing knowledge that Kyle is a sad-sack. Functional rather than exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So what do you think the song is called?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: April.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah! How did you—wait, that's not good, is it?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No, it's not.

jokes.text: 'Get out, Kyle.'
jokes.setup: Tom has just dressed up his dismissal of Kyle in sarcasm
jokes.punchline: He drops the pretense entirely and just bluntly tells Kyle to leave — the sudden plainness is funnier than any elaborate insult
jokes.explanation: Three words, maximum comedy. The economy score is perfect — stripping away all politeness and just issuing a flat eviction order is a great punchline to the preceding sarcasm beat. Quick but punchy.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm 21 now, which means I'm officially an adult. I can vote, I can serve on a jury, and I can drink alcohol responsibly.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: So obviously I'm going to get tattoos, stay up until 3 AM on a school night, and see how many shots I can do before I black out.

jokes.text: Andy wrote a song for April named after a month — April guesses 'April?' and Andy says no, then admits 'That would have been way better'
jokes.setup: Andy is being coy about the song title, saying it's 'named after a month out of the year'
jokes.punchline: April immediately and logically guesses her own name/birth month; Andy says no — then immediately concedes that would have been the better choice
jokes.explanation: A beautifully constructed two-beat joke. Andy's earnest incompetence — writing a song for April, about April, not naming it April — is perfectly Andy. Then his instant admission that her suggestion was better undercuts his romantic gesture without malice. It's charming, character-specific, structurally tight, and reveals sweetness underneath the stupidity. One of the episode's best jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: *evil laugh* Mwahahaha!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You sounded like a chimp.

jokes.text: Andy offers to rewrite the lyrics to fit the month of April, saying 'Um... Well, whatever. I can rewrite the lyrics.'
jokes.setup: Andy has written a song for April not named after April, admitted it would have been better, and now
jokes.punchline: He casually offers to rewrite the whole song as if it's no big deal — total obliviousness to how that undercuts his romantic gesture
jokes.explanation: A nice escalation of the previous joke. Andy's breezy willingness to completely redo the song deepens his lovable-idiot characterization. Not quite as sharp as the initial beat but still lands.

dialogue.speaker: Unknown official
dialogue.line: The event has been postponed indefinitely.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: When does indefinite end?

dialogue.speaker: Unknown official
dialogue.line: When it's no longer indefinite.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But how do we know when that is?

dialogue.speaker: Unknown official
dialogue.line: When we say it is.

jokes.text: April talking-head: 'Yes, I am 21 years old today. Which is the age that pretty much everyone agrees makes you an adult.'
jokes.setup: April's birthday is being celebrated
jokes.punchline: Her phrasing — 'pretty much everyone agrees' — is hilariously hedged, as if adulthood is a contested concept she's reluctantly conceding to consensus
jokes.explanation: The hedge 'pretty much everyone' is doing a lot of work. It's April's signature affect — reluctant, slightly contemptuous participation in social norms. The deadpan delivery would make this land perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know what? You're right. I can't fight the auditors. I'm just going to accept it and move on with my life.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Just kidding! I'm going to fight them with everything I have!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I know.

jokes.text: Ron does an evil villain laugh ('Mwah-ha-ha-ha / Ee-ah-ah-ah') and someone notes it 'Kind of sounded like a chimp there at the end'
jokes.setup: Ron is theatrically announcing his 'master plan' in a mockingly villainous way
jokes.punchline: His evil laugh devolves into chimp noises — the stoic Ron Swanson breaking character is inherently funny, and having someone call it out makes it better
jokes.explanation: Ron being silly is funny precisely because Ron is almost never silly. The chimp observation lands because it's delivered with total matter-of-factness, matching Ron's own register. Good character-based physical comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: What do you do when you're angry?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I go to my office, close the door, and I scream into a pillow for like forty-five minutes.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: That's very healthy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Then I take a nap on top of my desk. Then I wake up and I feel refreshed and ready to make government work for the people.

jokes.text: Leslie asks 'Until when?' / Ron: 'Indefinitely.' / Leslie: 'And when will that end?' / Ron: 'Later than now.' / Leslie: 'So this week probably?'
jokes.setup: Ron announces budget decisions are postponed 'indefinitely'
jokes.punchline: Leslie's escalating literal interpretation of 'indefinitely' — culminating in 'So this week probably?' — captures her relentless optimism/denial perfectly
jokes.explanation: A perfectly escalating exchange. Ron's 'later than now' is a gem of bureaucratic non-speak. Leslie's final 'so this week probably?' is the ideal character-specific punchline — her refusal to accept bad news is her core trait, and this exchange delivers it economically and with sharp escalation. Strong writing.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: So the rule is, you take half your age and add seven. That's the youngest you should date.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, so if you're 40, that's 20 plus 7, which is... 30?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: No, no. Half of 40 is 25, plus 7 is 34. Wait, that doesn't sound right either.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, I got 30. I'm pretty sure it's 30.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, you know what? 30 sounds right. Let's go with 30.

jokes.text: Leslie's anger-management technique revealed: 'We count backwards from 1,000 by sevens and we think of warm brownies'
jokes.setup: Ron sees Leslie getting worked up and asks 'What do we do when we get this angry?'
jokes.punchline: The technique is absurdly specific — counting by sevens from 1,000, plus warm brownies — suggesting Ron has had to deploy this many times before
jokes.explanation: The specificity of 'sevens from 1,000' implies this is a well-worn protocol between them, which is both funny and quietly touching. The brownies addition is a perfectly Leslie detail. The 'we' from Ron is the subtle key — he's done this many times.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Tom, I need dating advice. Who should I ask?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Well, you're asking me, so...

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh my God, that's a terrible idea. Never mind.

jokes.text: Leslie responds 'I'll wait for you to show up' mirroring Ron's instruction to go wait in her office
jokes.setup: Ron tells Leslie to go to her office and wait for the auditors
jokes.punchline: Leslie petulantly inverts the instruction, talking to Ron as if he's the one being sent away
jokes.explanation: A quick, functional comedic beat showing Leslie's stubbornness. Nothing special but the childish mirroring of authority is in character and gets a mild laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: I think it's great that we never fight. It means we have a really healthy relationship.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Actually, no. Couples that never fight are usually just repressing things. Healthy couples fight about stuff. They just do it in a respectful way.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: So you're saying we should fight more?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I'm saying we should fight about things that actually matter to us instead of pretending everything is fine all the time.

jokes.text: Tom asks Andy what's the youngest a girl can be 'that if we go out, I'm not a total scumbag'
jokes.setup: Tom is planning to hit on women at the club and has a specific ethical concern he needs quantified
jokes.punchline: Framing basic romantic ethics as a math problem with a scumbag threshold is an absurdly Tom-like approach to human decency
jokes.explanation: Tom consulting Andy on romantic ethics — arguably the last person who should be consulted — is itself funny. The 'total scumbag' calibration is a nice touch.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Every healthy relationship needs conflict. You need to fight sometimes.

dialogue.speaker: Mark
dialogue.line: Okay, I'll start hitting you.

jokes.text: Tom laboriously works out 'half of 29... add seven... that's only 20...' and trails off as he and Andy both arrive at the same answer about April's age
jokes.setup: Tom is doing the 'half your age plus seven' calculation out loud, seemingly not connecting it to anyone specific
jokes.punchline: Both men arrive at '21' simultaneously and exchange a meaningful look — the unstated implication being that they're both thinking about April on her 21st birthday
jokes.explanation: This is carefully engineered comedy. The audience does the math a beat ahead of Tom, realizes where this lands, and then the simultaneous arrival confirms it. The shared look is the punchline — it's a reaction beat that implicates both characters in a somewhat uncomfortable realization. Structurally elegant; the writers hide the setup in plain sight.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: State auditors? Oh God, oh God, oh God. This is it. This is how it ends. Not with a bang, but with a whimper and a tax audit.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Quick, someone hide all the office supplies I've been taking home! And my browser history! Why would they need my browser history?!

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I'm going to prison. I'm definitely going to prison. I've seen Oz. I'm not cut out for this.

jokes.text: Tom asks if he can date someone younger than the formula allows. Andy says: 'Please! You totally can.' Talking head: 'That probably means it isn't okay.'
jokes.setup: Tom asks for permission to go below the minimum age; Andy gives enthusiastic approval
jokes.punchline: Talking-head confessional reveals Tom knows Andy's endorsement is meaningless or counterindicative
jokes.explanation: The confessional topper is the best part: Tom is self-aware enough to know that Andy's approval is actually a red flag. The structure is tight — enthusiastic approval followed by immediate undermining. Good use of the mockumentary format.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: This is incredible. I have never seen anything like this before. This office tour is the most amazing experience of my entire life. Look at these fluorescent lights! Do you see how they illuminate the room? That is craftsmanship. And this carpet—it's so... carpeted. I'm getting emotional.

jokes.text: Jerry enters worried about being fired: 'Oh God, they're gonna fire people, aren't they? I am two years from my pension.'
jokes.setup: The auditors are arriving and the staff is nervous
jokes.punchline: Jerry's very first contribution to the conversation is entirely self-interested panic about his pension — pure Jerry
jokes.explanation: A reliable Jerry beat. His immediate pivot to self-preservation (pension) is character-consistent, but this joke type is well-worn territory for the character and doesn't elevate beyond its archetype.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: When I first met Chris, his positivity was so blinding I thought he was either a robot or a very handsome lighthouse.

jokes.text: Leslie says 'maybe these people are very helpful and pleasant--' and is immediately cut off by Chris Traeger entering with maximum enthusiasm
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to optimistically predict the auditors might not be bad
jokes.punchline: The auditors walk in and Jerry responds 'Ha! Death!' — perfect comedic timing of someone's worst fear being instantly confirmed even as Leslie is mid-reassurance
jokes.explanation: Jerry's 'Ha! Death!' is a great instinctive reaction — his immediate doom-reading of these strangers. The structural comedy of Leslie being cut off mid-optimism is clean and well-timed.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: We need to make some serious budget cuts. It's like we're closing down the fun house at the carnival.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: The fun house?

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Yeah, you know, where everything's distorted and nothing makes sense? That's our current government.

jokes.text: Chris says Ron Swanson's full name reverently — 'Ron...Swanson' — and Ron visibly savors the moment
jokes.setup: Chris is introduced to Ron and repeats his name slowly and with apparent reverence
jokes.punchline: Ron's implied reaction — basking in the gravitas of hearing his own name spoken that way — is a perfect Ron Swanson beat (implied from context)
jokes.explanation: This is excellent character comedy dependent almost entirely on what Ron DOESN'T say. Chris's name-repetition habit plus Ron's ego creates a perfect collision. The pause and register of the delivery make this a visual/reaction gag. Great introductory moment for both characters.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Ron, I've been looking at the department budget, and there's a lot of waste here.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Of course there is. Government is a swamp.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Well, I'm thinking we could cut some positions, streamline operations...

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Now you're speaking my language.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Finally, someone who understands that government should be smaller, leaner, more efficient. I've been dreaming of this day.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Pass me those pork cracklins.

jokes.text: Chris says 'There is quite literally nothing I would rather have in the world than a tour of the parks and recreation department of the great city of Pawnee led by Ron Swanson.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks if Chris and Ben would like a tour
jokes.punchline: Chris's response is so effusively enthusiastic — including the full bureaucratic department name — that it lands as absurdist character comedy; Ben's 'I don't think that's a great idea' suggests normal people find this overwhelming
jokes.explanation: Chris's positivity set up well here — the full department name spoken with reverence is the comedic peak. Ben's quiet protest as the straight man is a good counterpoint. Good character introduction but slightly over-long.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What is Jerry's actual value to this department?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, Jerry is the backbone of this department. Without Jerry, this office would fall apart. He's irreplaceable, he's essential, he's basically the Beyoncé of Parks and Rec.

jokes.text: Chris confessional: 'Chris is the most positive state budget auditing consultant I've ever met. I mean, I made eye contact with him, and it was like...staring into the sun.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is describing Chris in a talking-head interview
jokes.punchline: 'Staring into the sun' — the hypnotic intensity of Chris's positivity rendered as a physical danger
jokes.explanation: A quotable, efficient simile. The sun metaphor perfectly captures Chris's overwhelming positivity as something that can't be looked at directly. Delivered in Leslie's earnest register it's even funnier. Economy is excellent — the image does all the work.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: We're not here to save the world. We're here to do a little good each day. And if we're lucky, people notice. That's it. That's the whole thing. We're basically a band-aid on a gunshot wound, but we keep showing up with the band-aid anyway.

jokes.text: Chris's 'broken carousel' speech to the staff: 'Think of the government as a broken down carousel. We're gonna slap on a new coat of paint... and get those happy kids back up on the horses where they belong!'
jokes.setup: Chris is explaining the auditing team's mission to the worried Pawnee government staff
jokes.punchline: The carousel metaphor — cheerful, twee, and completely at odds with what auditors actually do (fire people and slash budgets) — is perfectly calibrated to Chris's blind optimism
jokes.explanation: The carousel image is charming and slightly unhinged. It establishes Chris as someone who wraps devastating news in such pretty packaging that no one knows they're being devastated. The 'yeah... okay... there it is' crowd response is a nice understated button.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Does the building have feelings?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Well, I mean, it's possible. Everything has feelings. I once cried for three hours because I thought a lamp looked sad.

jokes.text: Ben, one-on-one with Leslie, opens with 'I really like your shirt' before pivoting to asking where the waste is in her department
jokes.setup: Ben has pulled Leslie aside, presumably to discuss the audit
jokes.punchline: Opening with an awkward compliment before asking a hard question — it's Ben's fumbling attempt at small talk before going into budget-assassin mode
jokes.explanation: A small but effective character moment for Ben — the compliment is awkward and transactional, revealing his social stiffness. The pivot to 'where do you think there's waste' is an efficient punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So I was thinking we should go camping sometime, get to know each other better.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: But I realize how that sounds. I'm not trying to... you know. I just want to bond with you as a friend and coworker.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: We can bring other people! It'll be totally normal and not weird at all.

jokes.text: Immediate cut to two different talking heads — Leslie: 'There is none' / a colleague immediately after: 'Where do I start?'
jokes.setup: Ben asks where there's waste in the department
jokes.punchline: The juxtaposition of Leslie's defensive 'there is none' cut immediately against a colleague's 'where do I start?' is a classic mockumentary structure joke
jokes.explanation: A textbook mockumentary cut joke executed cleanly. The form is familiar but the execution is crisp — Leslie's certainty punctured instantly. High economy score because two words demolish Leslie's claim entirely.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Actually, now that it's legal, I'm not interested anymore.

jokes.text: Tom confessional: 'What exactly will you be cutting? And how much of it, and can I watch you doing it while eating pork cracklins?'
jokes.setup: Tom is asked about the auditors' plans
jokes.punchline: Tom's question escalates from legitimate concern to the weirdly specific 'pork cracklins' — he's eager to watch the carnage as entertainment while snacking
jokes.explanation: The 'pork cracklins' detail is perfect — unexpected and specific enough to feel like a real thing Tom would bring. Tom's schadenfreude about his colleagues' potential suffering while snacking is deeply in-character. A very Tom joke.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I know the guy who invented the Frito Lay.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.line: Wow, that's impressive!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, we're pretty tight. He calls me all the time.

dialogue.speaker: Woman
dialogue.line: What do you guys talk about?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Mostly chip flavors.

jokes.text: Ben asks what Tom can tell him about Jerry Gergich; Leslie calls him 'one of the best people on the planet' and says firing him would cause a revolt
jokes.setup: Ben is asking about potentially cutting personnel
jokes.punchline: Leslie's defense of Jerry — 'universally adored,' 'would cause a revolt' — is absurdly over the top for a character viewers know is treated terribly by everyone in the office
jokes.explanation: A solid running-gag deployment — Leslie's ironically glowing defense of Jerry contrasts with his perpetual mistreatment. Requires knowledge of the character dynamic to fully land. Functional rather than exceptional.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'You're a jerk.' Ben: 'I'm sorry?' Leslie: 'Easy.'
jokes.setup: Ben tells Leslie he'll just work from spreadsheets after she protests his attitude
jokes.punchline: Leslie blurts 'you're a jerk' and then, as if catching herself, says 'Easy' — apparently telling herself to calm down, but it sounds like she's calling him that too
jokes.explanation: The self-correction that sounds like an additional insult is a tight little comedic structure. Leslie's barely-controlled outrage is classic Leslie — she holds it together just long enough to make the situation worse.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Andy! Oh my God, hi!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Ann! Hey! How've you been?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Good, good. You look... really good actually.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Thanks! You too.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: No, I mean like, really good. Like, did you work out? Your arms look insane.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I mean, I've been going to the gym...

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: It shows. It really shows. Do you think I look good?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You always look good, Ann.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: But do I look GOOD good? Like, good enough that you regret breaking up with me?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, I think you've had enough to drink.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'This building has feelings? Maybe. There's a lot of history in this one, maybe it does.'
jokes.setup: Ben sarcastically asks 'This building has feelings?' after Leslie says her team has 'real feelings'
jokes.punchline: Leslie takes the sarcastic question seriously and genuinely considers whether the building has feelings — this is not a joke to her
jokes.explanation: A great Leslie moment — her passion for government and civic institutions is so deep she actually contemplates the emotional life of a municipal building. The joke only works with Leslie because she would genuinely mean it.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Do you think I was a good girlfriend to Chris? Like, was I supportive enough? Did I make him feel valued? Because sometimes I wonder if I could have been more attentive to his emotional needs, and I just really need to know if you think he felt loved.

jokes.text: Tom asks in confessional: 'What's a not-gay way to ask him to go camping with me?'
jokes.setup: Tom is apparently very impressed by Chris Traeger and wants to spend more time with him
jokes.punchline: Tom's framing of wanting a male friendship as a social problem requiring careful navigation — while also being slightly oblivious — is a quick, punchy self-revelation
jokes.explanation: Short and punchy. Tom is immediately smitten with Chris, and the camping question reveals he's processing a man-crush through a slightly ridiculous filter. Economy is high — it's one question, complete joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I feel like I've invested so much in this relationship with Andy, and I'm just not seeing the returns I expected.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: It's like I put in all this effort to help him grow as a person, and he's still just... Andy.

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio greets Tom with 'Lookin' hot, big T' followed by performing a little song/dance: '♪ throw them bones ♪'
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio arrives at the club
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio's entrance is pure chaos energy — the nickname, the spontaneous fragment of song — establishing him as someone who lives in a personal music video
jokes.explanation: Jean-Ralphio's first appearance in the episode is purely character comedy — his energy is the joke. The spontaneous song fragment is his calling card. Effective but dependent entirely on character.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Okay, so I'm thinking, if I wine her up at 7, dinner at 8, we're back here by 10:30, she's had two glasses of wine, her guard is down, we're listening to some Al Green, I'm looking at her like this... and boom, I'm in.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: But what if she orders the halibut? That's gonna throw off my whole timeline.

jokes.text: April says now that drinking is legal she's 'kind of lost interest'
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio brings April a birthday shot, presumably her first legal one
jokes.punchline: April has apparently been drinking illegally — the appeal was the illegality; now that it's permitted, she's bored by it
jokes.explanation: This is a genuinely excellent April joke. The inversion — most people celebrate being finally allowed to drink legally; April is disappointed by permission — is perfectly her character. It's contrarian, logical within her worldview, and delivered deadpan. High character integration because literally no other character on this show could deliver this line authentically. One of the episode's best.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: I showed up at her house every day for a week. Well, I thought it was her house. Turned out it was the wrong house, but the lady who lived there was into me, so it worked out. We did it on her kitchen table.

jokes.text: Ann asks 'You wanna get super drunk?' and Leslie responds 'I really do.' — then they immediately start looking for their friend
jokes.setup: Ann and Leslie are commiserating over a hard day — the park is on hold, Leslie talked to Mark
jokes.punchline: The directness of the request and immediate agreement, delivered without embarrassment, is endearing and funny in its bluntness
jokes.explanation: A quick warm beat that reveals the friendship. Not a complex joke but the economy and delivery make it land. The directness — 'super drunk' — is the best word choice here.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Andy, I've been flirting with you all day.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh cool, that's nice. Hey, did you see the game last night?

jokes.text: Trish (Miss Pawnee) is introduced and someone says 'I was instrumental in getting Trish crowned Miss Pawnee. What was your talent again? Oh, yeah. Looking amazing.'
jokes.setup: Tom brags about his role in getting Miss Pawnee crowned
jokes.punchline: The 'talent' reveal — 'looking amazing' — deflates the pageant pretense while simultaneously being pure Tom (he finds this a legitimate talent)
jokes.explanation: Efficient joke about beauty pageants and Tom's shallow aesthetic values. The self-answering question format is clean. The comedy is mild — not groundbreaking — but the character specificity saves it.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, what's that guy's name? Jean... Jean...

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Jean-Claude Van Damme?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: No wait... Jean-Ralphio!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: No, I'm thinking of Ralph Macchio. The Karate Kid guy.

jokes.text: Tom hits on women at the bar: 'Hey, ladies. Is there anything you desire at all besides me?' / 'I'm serious, though. Um, are you into me?'
jokes.setup: Tom approaches women at the party using his signature style
jokes.punchline: The complete absence of irony in his delivery — he thinks the joke opener IS the pickup line and then confirms he's serious — is cringe comedy at its most precise
jokes.explanation: The escalation from self-deprecating opener to sincere question is very Tom. The non-reaction from the women (implied) and the 'I'm serious, though' makes it cringe-funny. His obliviousness to how this lands is the engine.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I've been keeping track of my pickup attempts. I'm up to 847.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, that's just my phone bill. Never mind, I'm starting over.

jokes.text: Reaction beat — implied physical comedy: someone has to chug a drink and the crowd chants 'Chug that bitch! Oh, rules are rules.'
jokes.setup: The party is escalating; some kind of drinking game rule has been broken
jokes.punchline: The cheerful, rule-focused 'oh, rules are rules' immediately following 'chug that bitch' is the comedic contrast — treating a crude demand as a matter of principled adherence to protocol
jokes.explanation: A background party gag. The contrast between the crude imperative and the prim justification is the joke. Not deeply crafted but functional crowd energy. Low character integration because it could happen at any party on any show.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm not drunk. I'm just... I have a very rare condition where I can't pronounce words correctly and I walk into things.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Also I'm pretty sure I just called Ben 'Brenda' four times.

jokes.text: Andy seeing April in her party dress: 'You look amazing. Do a twirl. This is beautiful.' April refusing each escalation: 'No. No. Don't look at me.'
jokes.setup: Andy sees April dressed up for her birthday party
jokes.punchline: April's protests ('don't look at me') conflict with her obvious pleasure at Andy's attention — and Andy's relentless warmth against her practiced indifference creates the comedic tension
jokes.explanation: A lovely character beat that is also funny. April's contradictory behavior — protesting while clearly savoring the attention — is classic April. Andy's unguarded warmth is the engine. The 'do a twirl' is a perfect Andy escalation. Charming and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know what, Ben? I'm going to be honest with you because I'm drunk and that's when I tell the truth. I don't like you. I think you're pretentious and boring and you have no sense of humor.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Oh. Okay.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And your sweater vests are stupid.

jokes.text: Andy offers to get April a drink, catches himself ('wait'), and then brightly declares 'Yeah, I can swing it.' — remembering he's a part-owner of the bar
jokes.setup: Andy offers to buy April a drink, momentarily second-guesses if he can afford it
jokes.punchline: His self-reminder that he part-owns the bar lands as endearing dumbness — he forgot his own financial situation
jokes.explanation: A quick Andy beat — his delightful re-discovery of his own bar ownership. Doesn't overstay its welcome. Character-specific without being exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Wow, Leslie, that was really professional. You're such a great role model for workplace conduct.

jokes.text: April orders 'Whiskey. Neat.' and Andy responds 'Wow, you're not messing around.' April: 'No. I'm not.'
jokes.setup: Andy offers to get April a drink for her birthday
jokes.punchline: April ordering the most austere drink possible on her 21st birthday — and the weight she puts behind 'No. I'm not.' — is perfectly in character and slightly ominous in a funny way
jokes.explanation: Tight and well-executed. 'Whiskey. Neat.' is two words that say everything about April's persona. The confirmation 'No. I'm not.' given gravely is perfect. Economy score is very high — this is maximum character revelation per syllable.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Oh God, what happened last night?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Who... who did I...?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Hey, good morning! How's the head?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Tom? Oh no. Oh no, no, no. Please tell me we didn't...

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Didn't what? We just danced a little, you told me I was your favorite person in the office, then you threw up in a planter.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That's it? That's all that happened?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Well, you also kissed me. Twice.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I kissed you?!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: And me! Don't forget about me!

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie?! Oh God, I'm going to die.

jokes.text: Ann asks Andy 'Was I a good girlfriend?' / Andy: 'Ann, you were an awesome girlfriend.' / Ann: 'Really?' / Andy: 'Yeah... I mean, I was the screwup.' / Ann: 'Yeah, you were.'
jokes.setup: Ann seeks reassurance from her ex; Andy nobly falls on his sword
jokes.punchline: Ann's immediate 'Yeah, you were' — not a moment of hesitation — undercuts the romantic softness of the scene completely. She agrees a little too fast.
jokes.explanation: The comedic beat is Ann's instant agreement. The expected response would be 'oh no, you weren't that bad' — instead Ann concurs immediately, which lands as honest and funny in equal measure. The structure is clean: setup of nobility, punchline of immediate affirmation.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: Okay, here's what you need. Vitamin B complex, magnesium, potassium, NAD+, CoQ10, and a probiotic with at least 50 billion live cultures.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: You take all of these, you'll live to be 187 years old.

jokes.text: Ann confessional: 'I loved Andy. Loved him. Loved Andy. He was a totally helpless baby when we met. I dated him for three years. Now he's an adult with a job. And some other girl is gonna reap the rewards of my hard work? That's bull[bleep].'
jokes.setup: Ann is watching Andy be sweet and charming at the party
jokes.punchline: Ann's simmering resentment — framed as a labor-relations complaint about Andy's personal growth — culminates in 'that's bull[bleep].' The bleep makes it funnier.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout jokes. Ann framing romantic investment as labor — 'reap the rewards of my hard work' — is a genuinely original and true-to-life comedic insight. The triple 'loved Andy / loved him / loved Andy' is a funny rhythmic build. The bleep on the final expletive is a perfect button. This is well-earned, original, and character-specific. Meets the 8+ bar clearly.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, I'm sorry. You are like a beautiful flower, and I have been a terrible gardener who has let you wilt and—

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, just say it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You're fat.

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio's story about waiting outside a woman's house for five days: 'Turns out it was the wrong house. She loved the story anyway. We got to third base. Over the pants.'
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio tells Andy about his persistence with women
jokes.punchline: Three escalating beats: (1) five days outside her house, (2) wrong house entirely, (3) still worked — 'got to third base. Over the pants.' The final deflation is the button.
jokes.explanation: Three-beat structure executed beautifully. The escalation from unhinged devotion to farcical error to somehow successful outcome is classically comedic. The final 'over the pants' deflation is a perfectly calibrated anti-climax. Jean-Ralphio at his most Jean-Ralphio. Meets the 8+ bar for structure and delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I can't take my vitamins today.

dialogue.speaker: Chris
dialogue.line: I read that one batch might have been manufactured in a facility that also processes nuts, and I'm not even allergic to nuts, but what if I develop an allergy? What if the vitamins give me the allergy?

jokes.text: Tom gives April his Remy Martin 'for your birthday' — after she expressed interest in Jean-Ralphio; Tom's confessional: 'I thought she liked me. I guess I'm super bad at picking up signals.'
jokes.setup: Tom has been watching April interact with Jean-Ralphio and misread the situation
jokes.punchline: Tom's sad realization — 'super bad at picking up signals' — after all his bluster about being a romantic genius who'll get 1-4 girlfriends tonight
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback to Tom's opening confidence. His vulnerable admission, delivered as a genuine insight ('I guess I'm super bad at picking up signals'), is funnier than if he were self-aware. The Remy Martin offering as a consolation gift is also sweet and sad.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So Ann got drunk and blacked out, and I had to take care of her. Which is weird because usually it's the other way around.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: No it's not.

jokes.text: Tom confessional: 'But that Ralph Macchio guy's a total douche.'
jokes.setup: Tom has just admitted he can't read signals
jokes.punchline: He immediately reasserts dignity by attacking Jean-Ralphio — calling him by the wrong name (Ralph Macchio is a different celebrity entirely)
jokes.explanation: The wrong-name insult is a precise comedic choice. Tom calling Jean-Ralphio 'Ralph Macchio' (the Karate Kid actor) suggests he doesn't even care enough to remember his name. One line, two jokes simultaneously — the insult and the error. Well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What is this? A hundred and forty-seven dollars?

dialogue.speaker: Bartender
dialogue.line: You had a lot of cosmos.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I don't drink cosmos!

dialogue.speaker: Bartender
dialogue.line: The receipt says you ordered seven.

jokes.text: Jean-Ralphio frantically searching the bar demanding 'Did I give you a bottlecap? Excuse me. Did I give you a bottlecap?' / 'Who the [bleep] did I give a bottlecap to?'
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio earlier planted a bottlecap as part of his seduction strategy
jokes.punchline: He's completely lost track of who he gave it to — the elaborate 'system' has broken down entirely; he's now spiraling through the bar demanding it back
jokes.explanation: A perfect callback payoff. The methodical seduction strategy has collapsed into chaos. Jean-Ralphio manically demanding his bottlecap back from strangers is funnier than anything he did in the setup. The escalating desperation ('Who the [bleep] did I give a bottlecap to?') is excellent. One of the episode's better physical-comedy/callback moments.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: A 43-way? That's impossible. I mean, mathematically, logistically... I don't even know where you'd start. And more importantly, I'd hate to disappoint 43 women.

jokes.text: Ann: 'You know what's weird? How thirsty I get when I'm weird.' Pause. 'When I'm drunk.'
jokes.setup: Drunk Ann is trying to say something about being thirsty
jokes.punchline: She says 'weird' instead of 'drunk,' catches herself, corrects it — the self-correction while clearly drunk is the joke
jokes.explanation: The Freudian slip where 'weird' and 'drunk' get confused is a good drunk-person gag — it's specific enough to feel observed and Ann's straight-faced self-correction makes it land. 'You know what's weird? How thirsty I get when I'm weird' is accidentally a decent sentence.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: When I was a teenager, I thought I had all the answers. I was going to change the world, fix every problem, make everything perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Now I realize that teenage me was an idiot.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: But at least he cared.

jokes.text: April to a drunk Leslie: 'Ben the jerk is here.' / Leslie: 'Who are?' / April: 'That one. The one coming over here. Get ready.'
jokes.setup: Ben approaches the group at the party
jokes.punchline: 'Who are?' — April points at Ben and Leslie's drunk processing of information is hilarious; April's 'get ready' treating it like an approaching battle is also funny
jokes.explanation: Leslie's drunk syntax ('who are?') is a nice detail. April's battle-prep framing is fun. Together they make a decent comedic beat without being outstanding.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: When a politician fails, they're basically done. They become a lobbyist, or they go on Fox News, or they write a book nobody reads.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: But if you really screw up? Really embarrass yourself? You have to go on a morning show and talk about your feelings.

jokes.text: Leslie tells Ben to leave: 'I just talked to everybody in this bar and nobody wants you here.' then after he leaves, Ann says 'Leslie, that was so professional. I'm so proud of you.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has just aggressively told Ben to get out of the party in a completely unprofessional way
jokes.punchline: Ann's straight-faced 'that was so professional, I'm so proud of you' is pure sarcasm — but in this friend group, it's delivered warmly, making it funnier
jokes.explanation: The delivery makes this — Ann's mock-pride is warm rather than cutting, which is very Parks. The irony works because Leslie probably also believes it was professional. Clean structure: disaster followed by deadpan praise.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, you performed 'Ice Ice Baby' at a formal state dinner?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I was 16 and thought I was making a bold political statement.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: By rapping Vanilla Ice?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: The Governor was not amused.

jokes.text: Leslie may have made out with someone the night before and doesn't know who: 'I just had this feeling when I woke up this morning like I definitely kissed somebody.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is asking Ann for help piecing together what happened
jokes.punchline: The vagueness is the joke — not 'I kissed someone and don't remember who,' but a more impressionistic 'I had this feeling like I definitely kissed somebody' — hungover epistemological uncertainty
jokes.explanation: A good setup for the running mystery of who Leslie kissed. The 'feeling' phrasing is authentically funny — she's working from sensory memory rather than actual memory. A good engine for later jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Do you think I blacked out and did something crazy?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Good God, woman, no.

jokes.text: Ann sees Jerry at the office and checks: 'Yeah, crazy...' then to Leslie, after Jerry leaves: 'So it's not Jerry.'
jokes.setup: Ann is trying to figure out who Leslie kissed; she sees Jerry and subtly gathers intel
jokes.punchline: The reveal 'so it's not Jerry' — delivered with obvious relief — implies that Jerry was a serious enough suspect that Ann had to investigate, which is dark comedy about Jerry's status
jokes.explanation: The 'not Jerry' conclusion as a moment of relief is quietly devastating and funny. That Jerry had to be eliminated as a suspect via covert observation says everything. The economy is excellent — 'so it's not Jerry' does all the work.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: How am I supposed to contact you?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Just call me on my phone.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I don't have your number.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Well, I'll give you my number... but only if you give me yours first.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: That's... that's how phone numbers work.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: No, I mean give me your actual phone. Then I can call myself on it and you'll have my number.

jokes.text: Chris offers Leslie a vitamin from a large collection: 'B12? Evening primrose oil? Willow bark? Magnesium?' Leslie declines, he insists it's good for hangovers, she relents.
jokes.setup: Leslie arrives at the office the morning after the party
jokes.punchline: Chris's wellness arsenal — the volume and specificity of supplements — characterizes him as someone for whom nutrition is a religion
jokes.explanation: A good extension of Chris's character comedy. The escalating list is a standard joke form but works because 'willow bark' is unexpectedly archaic. The hangover context makes Leslie's reluctant 'okay I'll take one' funny.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A government shutdown? But... but I love government. I love the people in government. I love the process of government. How can government shut down? It's like asking the sun to stop being hot, or asking me to stop being awesome.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: This is fine. Everything is fine. I'm fine.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: *humming intensifies into full circus calliope music*

jokes.text: Chris confessional: 'Scientists believe that the first human being who will live 150 years has already been born. I believe I am that human being.'
jokes.setup: Chris is explaining his health philosophy
jokes.punchline: The leap from 'scientists believe' (a real claim) to 'I believe I am that human being' (maximum narcissistic delusion delivered with complete sincerity) is the joke
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the episode. It's a perfect character-establishing line for Chris Traeger — positive thinking taken to its logical, insane extreme. The structure is flawless: real scientific claim → personal claim of exemption from mortality. Highly quotable. Economy is near-perfect: two sentences, fully realized worldview. The confidence of 'I believe I am that human being' with no hedge is the comedic peak. Meets the 8+ bar easily and arguably higher.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: ♪ April, April, your birthday's in July... ♪

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: My birthday is in December.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I know, but July rhymes with 'guy' and you're... a guy. A cool guy.

jokes.text: Leslie tells Ben: 'You may hold my fate in your hands like a small bird, but I still think you're an ass.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is trying to apologize professionally but can't quite contain her true feelings
jokes.punchline: The contrast between the delicate, literary 'small bird' metaphor and the blunt 'I still think you're an ass' is the joke — Leslie's earnestness and hostility coexist perfectly
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most quotable lines. The structural contrast — tender metaphor + brutal directness — is very well-crafted. It's also deeply Leslie: she would choose 'small bird' as a metaphor for power dynamics, and she would follow it with an insult because she genuinely can't help herself. Meets the 8+ bar. Highly quotable.

jokes.text: Ben's response to 'you're an ass': 'You wanna get a beer?' / Leslie: 'It's like 10:30 in the morning.' / Ben: 'Yeah. You seem like you could use a beer.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has just insulted Ben to his face after attempting an apology
jokes.punchline: Ben's immediate pivot to beer — not arguing, not getting offended — is a perfect character reveal. His 'you seem like you could use a beer' confirms he's an attuned pragmatist
jokes.explanation: A strong character introduction beat for Ben. His non-reaction to the insult — pivoting immediately to a social solution — tells us a lot about him economically. The 10:30am timing note from Leslie makes his suggestion funnier and his 'you seem like you could use one' even better.

jokes.text: Chris calls out after Ben: 'Oh, oh, oh, oh. Don't keep him too long. I need someone to be here when I take my multivitamin. There's a choking hazard.'
jokes.setup: Ben is heading off to get a beer with Leslie
jokes.punchline: Chris's only concern is the choking hazard of taking a multivitamin alone — the health obsession played completely straight, implying Ben is his vitamin safety spotter
jokes.explanation: Excellent Chris character comedy. The idea that he needs a vitamin-safety buddy — and this is apparently a genuine concern, not a joke to him — extends his health-obsession characterization perfectly. The callback to his supplement collection in joke 50 adds texture.

jokes.text: Ann reveals to Leslie that they didn't make out — but drags out the revelation for maximum suspense: 'This is going to be so fun letting you dangle until I finally reveal that we did not make out.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has been desperate to know if she kissed someone; Ann has the information
jokes.punchline: Ann tells Leslie she's going to enjoy the suspense, then immediately tells her anyway — the announcement of a plan that is immediately abandoned is the joke
jokes.explanation: A nicely structured moment. Ann announcing her plan to tease and then immediately defusing it (by telling her the answer) is a fun anti-escalation. Leslie's 'oh [bleep]. Damn it.' at the not-kissing news is a perfect character beat — disappointed that nothing happened.

jokes.text: Ann talking head: 'For once, it's Ann who blacked out drunk and not Andy.' — Tom, apparently.
jokes.setup: Ann doesn't remember the previous night
jokes.punchline: Someone notes this is a reversal of the usual dynamic where Andy is the blackout drunk
jokes.explanation: A good character-history beat that contextualizes Ann and Andy's past. The flip of the expected dynamic is funny and the third-person 'Ann' usage suggests this is someone else's talking head about her. Economical.

jokes.text: Leslie's response to learning she did NOT make out with Ann: 'Oh, [bleep]. Damn it.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has been in agony over possibly having kissed someone
jokes.punchline: She's DISAPPOINTED that nothing happened — the expected relief is inverted; Leslie apparently wanted it to have happened
jokes.explanation: The inversion — relief expected, disappointment delivered — is a clean and well-executed misdirection. The economy is exceptional: two expletives deliver the entire emotional information. Leslie apparently regrets her own sobriety in this specific scenario.

jokes.text: Tom's bar tab revealed: '47 drinks last night. Ten cosmos, eight Smirnoff Ices, and everything else starts with the word pomegranate.' Bartender: 'Was it your bachelorette party?'
jokes.setup: Tom is settling his tab the morning after the party
jokes.punchline: 47 drinks is already absurd; the breakdown (Smirnoff Ices, pomegranate everything) characterizes Tom's tastes as feminized by bro-culture standards — hence the bartender's 'bachelorette party' guess
jokes.explanation: A great joke with two levels: (1) 47 drinks is an absurd number, (2) the drink choices are hysterical character-specific details. The 'everything else starts with the word pomegranate' is the best line. The bartender's bachelorette assumption is the perfect punchline — it reads Tom's drink order as coded femininity.

jokes.text: Tom explains: 'I invited a bunch of girls here last night, and they all put drinks on my tab. And then I went home alone. I'm not sure what happened.'
jokes.setup: The bartender asks if it was his bachelorette party; Tom explains the actual situation
jokes.punchline: 'I'm not sure what happened' — delivered with genuine puzzlement about an outcome that is utterly predictable
jokes.explanation: The genuine bafflement is the joke. Tom's lack of self-awareness — that inviting women somewhere and hitting on them doesn't mean they'll go home with you — is a perfectly Tom confusion. The 'I'm not sure what happened' lands because he truly doesn't know.

jokes.text: Bartender to Tom: 'What were you expecting was gonna happen, a 43-way?' / Tom: 'That would have been a little out of control. But awesome.'
jokes.setup: The bartender is pointing out the obvious flaw in Tom's plan
jokes.punchline: Tom doesn't reject the '43-way' premise — he says it would have been 'a little out of control. But awesome.' — he's sad it didn't happen, not that it was suggested
jokes.explanation: Tom's response is perfect — the mild objection ('a little out of control') followed by 'but awesome' confirms his worldview completely. He's not offended; he's wistful. Character integration is high because this is pure Tom.

jokes.text: Tom: 'The problem is I only have 15 penises. So there would have been 28 girls that were really upset with me.'
jokes.setup: Tom has agreed the 43-way would have been awesome but has a logistical concern
jokes.punchline: Tom calculates the disappointing math of a 43-way with deadpan seriousness, as if 15 penises is a fixed and known quantity and the 28 disappointed girls is the specific problem
jokes.explanation: This is the funniest line in the episode. The absurdist logic is impeccably constructed: Tom treats his (mythical) 15-penis inventory as a real constraint in a real math problem about romantic satisfaction. '28 girls that were really upset with me' is the perfect punchline — it's the number, not the concept, that's the joke. The delivery of this as a genuine concern, not a boast, is what makes it transcendent. Meets and arguably exceeds the 8+ bar. Comparable to the 'snip snap' reference in its absurdist escalation and high-impact delivery.

jokes.text: Andy asks the bartender out: 'Hey, uh, would you wanna get a drink tomorrow night?' / Bartender: 'Does it have to be here?' / Andy: 'No.' / Bartender: 'Then sure. I'm Lucy.'
jokes.setup: Andy has been helping settle Tom's tab and is now chatting with the bartender
jokes.punchline: Lucy's condition — 'does it have to be here?' — implies that she definitely doesn't want to go on a date where she works; it's also the easiest bar to clear, and Andy clears it
jokes.explanation: A charming and clean joke. Lucy's condition is a funny/realistic concern (not dating where you work). Andy solving the problem with a single 'no' is perfectly Andy — he's not trying to be smooth, it just works. A nice moment of Andy accidentally succeeding at romance.

jokes.text: Tom meets Lucy the bartender: 'Hey, uh, would you wanna get a drink tomorrow night?' Lucy: 'Does it have to be here?' Tom: 'No.' Lucy: 'Then sure.' — she gives him her number.
jokes.setup: Tom, fresh off a humiliating night, asks the bartender out
jokes.punchline: Her only condition is that they go somewhere else — meaning she's seen enough of his behavior at this bar to want a clean slate, but still says yes
jokes.explanation: The condition — not 'somewhere nicer' but specifically 'not here' — is a pointed commentary on what she witnessed without being cruel. Tom's surprised delight at this outcome after the night he had is a good character beat.

jokes.text: Ben reveals he was once the 18-year-old mayor of Partridge, Minnesota. Leslie: 'Why does that sound familiar?'
jokes.setup: Ben mentions he has experience in government — he ran for mayor of a small town
jokes.punchline: Leslie immediately recognizes it — this political scandal is apparently something she would know about from following local government closely
jokes.explanation: A good setup for the reveal to come. Leslie's recognition is funny because it confirms her encyclopedic knowledge of local government across the state — this is who she is. The 'why does that sound familiar' pause is well-used.

jokes.text: Ben explains: 'Here's the thing about 18-year-olds. They're idiots. So I pretty much ran the place into the ground after two months and got impeached. Worst part was, my parents grounded me.'
jokes.setup: Ben was 18 when he was elected mayor
jokes.punchline: The escalating humiliations: ran it into the ground → impeached → parents grounded him. The grounding is the perfect button — it recontextualizes a political scandal as a teenager getting punished
jokes.explanation: One of the best constructed jokes in the episode. Three-beat escalation: (1) ran it into the ground, (2) impeached, (3) parents grounded him. The third beat is the key — it reduces a serious political story to teenage domestic consequences, perfectly deflating the drama. 'Worst part was, my parents grounded me' is perfectly timed and highly quotable. Meets the 8+ bar clearly — comparable to the anchor examples in structure.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'What was that song you played at the swearing-in ceremony?' Ben: 'Whoomp! There it is is what it was, yeah.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is reading an article about the teenage mayor of Partridge
jokes.punchline: An 18-year-old choosing 'Whoomp! There It Is' as his mayoral swearing-in song is perfectly period-appropriate and ridiculous; Ben's slightly ashamed confirmation is the punchline
jokes.explanation: A great specific detail. The song choice is both accurate to the era and wildly inappropriate for a swearing-in ceremony. Ben's awkward confirmation — 'is what it was, yeah' — implies he knows how it sounds. A very good specific joke.

jokes.text: Leslie and Ben do 'Whoomp! There It Is' at the bar — they both know the song and sing along together awkwardly/delightedly
jokes.setup: Ben has just confessed to the 'Whoomp! There It Is' swearing-in ceremony
jokes.punchline: The natural progression — they both know the song, they do a bit of it together — is an unexpected moment of connection that's both funny and sweet
jokes.explanation: A nice moment of unexpected bonding. It's more sweet than funny, but there's a comedic element in two serious professionals breaking into a 90s hip-hop song at 10:30am at a bar. The rewatch bonus is for the relationship setup it provides.

jokes.text: Leslie and Ben toast and she does a 'Mr. Mayor' riff: 'Oh, no, please, Mr. Mayor. Let me.' Then they play 'Whoomp! There It Is' on a jukebox.
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben have connected over his teenage mayoral disaster
jokes.punchline: Leslie leans into the 'Benji Wyatt the Mayor' bit and they play his swearing-in song at the bar — the callback to 'Whoomp! There It Is' as a shared joke
jokes.explanation: A warm callback that serves character development as much as comedy. The joke is softer here but the shared laughter over the song cements the Leslie-Ben connection. The fact that they're bonding over his civic humiliation is characterful.

jokes.text: Leslie checks the last man on her list: 'Hey, Ron, did we make out last night?' / Ron: 'Good God, woman, no.'
jokes.setup: Leslie is systematically going through every man she knows to find who she kissed
jokes.punchline: Ron's 'Good God, woman' is the perfect reaction — it's not insulted, it's just maximum Ron Swanson offended dignity at the very premise
jokes.explanation: The payoff of the running mystery. The comedy is almost entirely in Ron's response — 'Good God, woman, no' is a perfect Ron Swanson line: four words, complete and total rejection, total dignity maintained. The question itself is the setup; Ron's horrified certainty is the punchline. Highly quotable and a great Ron moment. Meets the 8+ bar via character integration and economy.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'Okay. Well, that's it. That's all the men that I know.'
jokes.setup: Leslie has been through every man she knows and eliminated them all as kissing candidates
jokes.punchline: The sad finality of 'that's all the men that I know' — delivered with resignation — is both funny and faintly melancholy
jokes.explanation: A gentle, character-rich button on the running gag. Leslie's entire romantic world apparently consists of a handful of men, all of whom she's now eliminated. The deadpan understatement of saying this out loud lands warmly.

jokes.text: Chris appears and cheerfully greets Ann: 'Hey. Ann Perkins!' — with maximum enthusiasm for her full name
jokes.setup: Chris is introduced to Ann at the end of the party/night
jokes.punchline: Chris's habit of saying full names with reverent enthusiasm — established earlier with 'Ron... Swanson' — is now applied to Ann
jokes.explanation: A good callback to Chris's full-name-reverence habit. 'Ann Perkins!' becomes a running gag in the show. It's funnier in context — the enthusiasm is completely unearned by the situation, which is the joke.

jokes.text: Ann waking up in a cab, drunk, being told she's getting a cab by Leslie: 'Mm-mm-mm, mm-mm-mm. Mm.'
jokes.setup: Ann has apparently kissed someone at the party (implied); she is now extremely drunk and being ushered into a cab
jokes.punchline: Her non-verbal response — the 'mm-mm-mm' sounds — communicates total inebriated incapacity, which is the joke
jokes.explanation: A visual/physical comedy beat. Funny in context as the payoff of Ann being drunk all night, but dependent entirely on the performance rather than any writing craft. Below average for the episode.

jokes.text: Ann can't remember her own phone number but gave a stranger her phone: 'You have my phone number?' / 'No, you couldn't remember your phone number. But you gave me your phone.'
jokes.setup: Chris says he'll call Ann later; she asks if he has her number
jokes.punchline: Drunk Ann solved the phone number problem by giving away her phone — the escalation of drunk logic is perfect
jokes.explanation: A great drunk-logic joke. The escalating solution — can't remember number → give entire phone — is both funny and internally consistent with blackout reasoning. The reveal is efficiently delivered.

jokes.text: Leslie: 'I'm sorry, I just started hearing really loud circus music in my head. What did you say?' — in response to the government shutdown announcement
jokes.setup: Ben has just announced the entire Pawnee government will be shut down until further notice
jokes.punchline: Leslie's dissociation — hearing 'circus music' as her brain copes with devastating news — is a perfect Leslie response to catastrophe
jokes.explanation: A strong character joke. The circus music detail is specific and unexpected — Leslie's coping mechanism manifests as literal auditory hallucination. It's a great way to play the scene's dramatic stakes (government shutdown) for comedy without undercutting the drama. Very Leslie. Meets the 8+ bar through character integration and quotability.

jokes.text: Closing credits: Andy's song for April is revealed — 'November' — and the song is clearly about April, not November. Final card: 'That song is about April.'
jokes.setup: Early in the episode, Andy wrote April a song named after a month, didn't call it 'April', admitted April would have been better
jokes.punchline: The song is called 'November' — but the credits card confirms 'That song is about April.' — Andy's roundabout sincerity is made explicit in text
jokes.explanation: A beautiful episode-closing callback. The reveal that the song is called 'November' but is obviously about April completes the episode's Andy/April thread perfectly. The title card 'That song is about April' is the writers winking — it's completely unnecessary to state, which makes it funnier. The structural satisfaction of a cold-open joke paying off in the credits earns high scores. Sweet and funny simultaneously, which is Parks at its best.

tmdb_overview: Leslie is disappointed when her new park plans are put on hold by a visit from two state auditors. April has plans for Andy at her birthday party, and Ann tries to piece together a romantic mystery.
insight: Season finale stakes collapse under 49 rapid-fire character gags and absurdist chaos.
